content: 1. A comprehensive list of all TB Basic Management Units (BMUs) in the country should be maintained. Additionally, provincial and district TB officers, laboratory managers, and small survey teams (including National TB Program (NTP) staff) should conduct census and health facility assessments. 2. Records of notified TB cases for the year of assessment should be available in the national patientor case-based database. 3. TB case data from the national routine TB surveillance system should be disaggregated by age for the most recent year with complete data. 4. TB surveillance data must demonstrate internal consistency over time. If vital registration (VR) data are available, the following benchmarks should be met: Consistent trajectories in the same direction over time. Evidence of internal consistency at the national level over the past five years for the following indicators: Ratio of pulmonary to extrapulmonary TB cases. Ratio of male to female TB cases. Proportion of childhood TB cases among all TB cases. Year-to-year changes in case notification rates for all forms of TB. Year-to-year changes in case notification rates for new smear-positive TB cases. 5. If VR data are available, national-level TB mortality rates (HIV-negative TB) should be obtained from VR systems. If VR data are not available, national-level TB case data disaggregated by age, sex, type of disease, and case notification rates (for all forms and smear-positive TB cases) should be obtained from routine TB surveillance for the past five years. Subnational data should also be collected and examined where possible. 6. If available, national-level TB suspect registry data should be reviewed. 7. Legal and regulatory frameworks, national TB health reports, and policy documents should be reviewed to ensure alignment with international standards. 8. Inventory studies conducted within the past 10 years should be included in the assessment. 9. Vital registration systems should have high national coverage and quality. To meet this standard: The cause of death should be documented in at least 90% of total recorded deaths in either the national VR system or a sample VR system. Less than 10% of deaths should have ill-defined causes (e.g., ICD-9 codes 780-799 or ICD-10 codes R00-R99). 10. Surveillance data should provide direct measures of drug-resistant TB among new cases. To meet this standard, one of the following benchmarks must be satisfied: Rifampicin susceptibility status (positive/negative) should be documented for at least 75% of new pulmonary TB cases. Rifampicin susceptibility status should be documented for a nationally representative drug resistance survey of new pulmonary TB cases. 11. Surveillance systems should routinely collect data for a minimum set of variables for all reported TB cases, including: Age or age group. Sex. Year of registration. Bacteriological results. History of previous treatment. Anatomical site of disease. Patient identifier (for case-based systems). 12. National TB case definitions should align with WHO-recommended definitions to ensure logical consistency. These definitions should be documented in NTP manuals and policies and reviewed for consistency with WHO guidelines. 13. If the standard is not met, a national advisory group should review and revise current case definitions, update national guidelines, adapt recording and reporting systems (both paper and electronic), and update training materials accordingly. 14. In Kenya, the Division of Leprosy, Tuberculosis, and Lung Disease has developed guidelines consistent with WHO recommendations. These guidelines include clear case definitions for TB management, recording, and reporting, differentiating between laboratory-confirmed and clinical cases, new and previously treated cases, and pulmonary and extrapulmonary cases. 15. In the United States, the electronic case-based TB surveillance system spans all 50 states, the District of Columbia, and eight USA-affiliated island nations. Reporting occurs at city, county, and state levels, with standardized forms such as the Report of Verified Case of Tuberculosis (RVCT) used since 1985. The system meets all benchmarks and aligns with WHO guidelines. 16. In Uganda, the surveillance system is paper-based, with data collected at the facility level and aggregated at district and national levels. While some variables are captured for all cases, others, such as age and laboratory confirmation, are only routinely reported for specific case types (e.g., new smear-positive cases). As a result, this standard is only partially met. 17. Subnational reporting units must fulfill their obligations to report data to the national level. If not all units report, national data will be incomplete, compromising the accuracy of TB surveillance. 18. Paper-based systems following WHO guidelines rely on quarterly reports aggregated at TB BMUs. These reports are sent up the administrative chain, with aggregation occurring at each stage. National aggregates should be based on reports from 100% of BMUs. 19. If the standard is not met, key actions to address gaps should be described, and an estimated budget should be developed to support activities that bridge these gaps. 20. Revised TB recording and reporting forms and systems should be developed, and related training should be conducted to ensure the collection of the minimum data required to assess trends and consistency. This version maintains the technical rigor and specificity required for medical professionals while ensuring clarity and readability.
